agent: Claude Code (CLAUDE.md, this repository) — §9 "calling a process": real engine execution for the PROCESS mechanism
summary_for_principal: The engine can now actually RUN a step that calls another process, not just accept it as a valid definition. Both forms work: a step that calls a separately named, independently governed process, and one that carries its own small private workflow inline. Either way, the engine drives it itself — no separate approvals or hand-offs are invented, and if that inner workflow itself needs a person or an agent to do something, that request now correctly bubbles all the way up to whoever is running the outer process, tagged with exactly where it happened, so answering it and resuming works the same way it already does everywhere else. A call chain that nests too deep (default limit: 4 levels) is refused rather than allowed to run forever. A named process with no permission set up is refused before it is ever entered, the same protection every other step already has. One thing is deliberately NOT built yet: the spec allows a call to force which of the inner workflow's own branches it must take first; that is refused with a clear message rather than silently ignored, since guessing at it wrongly would be worse than saying no. Full test suite: 315 passing (310 before this + 5 new, each proving one of the behaviours above).

also.reason: Added StepOutcome.DEPTH_EXHAUSTED (§9.2) so a call-chain depth breach routes through the same outcome/routing machinery as any other STEP failure.

Five new tests: ref'd process call success (output/ending translation), inline process call with a nested hand-off resumed via report() against its own nested scope, depth-limit exhaustion, a ref'd child with no permission being refused before entry, and a control failure on the translated output routing via on_control_fail.
§9 ("calling a process"), §9.1-§9.3, §10.1/D14, §12.1 read as the authoritative shape this implementation must match; no spec text changed this run.

The immediately preceding run (D18) built the PROCESS-mechanism shape and explicitly named engine execution as its own follow-up action (n2 in that run's where_next.actions) — this run is that action, not new scope.

interpretation.ask_as_given: Please close the gap so that the engine could support the steps we've defined
interpretation.read_as: Build the actual engine execution path for the PROCESS mechanism (both ref'd and inline forms) — the running capability the immediately preceding run's own where_next.actions[1] named as still missing after the schema/model work landed. The prior turns in this conversation (agreeing to fold AGENTIC into PROCESS, keeping SKILL for the single-step case) already settled what a PROCESS-mechanism step means; this instruction is about making the engine able to run it, not about redesigning it further.

filled_in.gap: The instruction did not spell out several sub-questions §9 leaves as worked examples rather than fully pinned-down mechanics: where the call-chain depth limit comes from when unset, whether a ref'd child's own permission is checked once or on every resume, what happens when a call declares `path` (§9.1's route-forcing override), and what a completed child's state looks like when evaluating `result.outputs` paths.
filled_in.assumed: Resolved each by extending an existing, already-decided convention rather than inventing a new one: the depth default is spec §9.2's own stated default (4) via the already-scaffolded `defaults.max_depth`/`fmt_defaults.MAX_DEPTH`; a ref'd child's permission is checked once, at the point of delegation, the same way a Tool's own permission is checked once per dispatch rather than on every replay (D12's own precedent); `path` is refused outright (EngineRefusal) rather than silently ignored, since honouring it wrong would produce a running process silently taking the wrong branch, which is worse than a clean refusal naming the gap; and `result.outputs` is evaluated against {"state": <child's final state>} only, matching every worked example in the spec (all reference state.* paths) — nothing exercises inputs/host/steps in that position, so nothing was built for them.
filled_in.grounded_in: spec §9.1 ("path MAY name the option the child's first route must take; otherwise the child decides"), §9.2 ("default 4"), §10.1/D14 (permission checked before dispatch, not re-checked on every replay of an already-dispatched attempt).
filled_in.reversal_cost: Cheap for all four: `path` support is additive (nothing today depends on it being refused); the depth-limit source is read from one place (`_advance_process_call`) so swapping it costs one edit; permission-check timing and the result.outputs run-state shape are both internal to `_advance_process_call` and touch no caller-visible contract.

decisions.headline: §9 ("calling a process") is now real engine behaviour: a PROCESS-mechanism STEP — ref'd or inline — recursively drives a child scope via a generalised `_drive_scope`, and a nested hand-off resumes through the exact same `report()`/`decide()`/`skip()` entry points as a top-level one, with no separate "resume the child then cascade the parent" mechanism.
decisions.problem: WP-02 had always deferred "calling a process" past its own scope (this module's own header docstring named it explicitly), and the immediately preceding run built the declarable shape (`Mechanism.process`, `Mechanism.result`) without any engine that could run it. The principal then asked directly to close that remaining gap.
options_rejected: A separate function that, given a nested scope whose child just finished, walks back up and continues the parent from where it left off. Rejected: `report()`/`decide()`/`skip()` already restart `_drive_scope` from the scope's own top segment on every call (§12.1's own stateless-replay contract) — natural replay-and-delegate-down already reaches and continues the correct nested level, so a second mechanism would duplicate that guarantee under a different name and risk drifting from it.

Re-checking a ref'd child process's own permission on every resume of an in-flight nested call. Rejected: once the parent's own STEP records a terminal attempt for the call (success or failure), `_advance_step`'s existing attempt-history branch returns without ever re-entering the PROCESS-mechanism dispatch branch at all — matching how a CODE Tool's permission is checked once per dispatch attempt, not on every subsequent replay of an already-recorded one.

Treating a PROCESS-mechanism call's controls/repair/retry as a special case with its own logic. Rejected: the translated output is routed through the exact same `check_controls` + `_record_step_result` machinery a CODE dispatch uses (spec gives controls no special treatment per mechanism kind), accepting as a known, disclosed nuance that a repair/retry fallthrough on an already-ended child just idempotently re-observes the same result rather than re-running the child's own logic (see untouched item below).
decisions.cost_to_change: Low — every new piece (`_ScopeDef`, `_resolve_scope`, `_drive_scope`, `_advance_process_call`, `NextAnswer.scope`) is additive; no existing call site's external contract changed (next_/report/decide/skip keep their prior signatures, and 310 pre-existing tests pass unmodified).

evidence.claim: A ref'd PROCESS-mechanism call correctly recurses into the named child process, and the child's final state is translated back through `mechanism.result.outputs`/`.endings` into the calling STEP's own output and route.

An inline (`process:`) PROCESS-mechanism call whose child hands off (a SKILL Tool inside it) bubbles that hand-off up carrying the CHILD's own nested scope string (e.g. "root/call-inline"), and report() against exactly that scope both completes the child and continues the parent to its own ending — proving the no-separate-cascade design actually holds, not just that it was reasoned through.

A call chain deeper than the process's own `max_depth` (forced to 0 for the test) never delegates into the child at all — it routes via `on_depth_exhausted` (or the format default), the same as any other STEP failure.

A ref'd child process with no `permission` declared is refused (FORBIDDEN, routed via on_forbidden) before the child is ever entered — the CountingAdapter standing in for the child's own Tool recorded zero calls.

A control declared on the CALLING Tool checks the translated output the same way it checks any other Tool's output, and a failure there routes via on_control_fail's `then` exactly like a CODE dispatch's control failure would.
The full pre-existing suite (310 tests) passes unchanged after this rewrite, and 5 new tests bring the total to 315, 0 failed.

untouched.divergence: §9.1: "`path` MAY name the option the child's first route must take; otherwise the child decides." This engine refuses (EngineRefusal) any PROCESS-mechanism call that declares `path`, rather than honouring the override.
untouched.why_not_now: No fixture, scenario, or corpus process in this repository declares `path` on a process call, and implementing it correctly needs the child's very first ROUTE resolution to be forced rather than evaluated — a distinct piece of logic this run had no real case to build or test against. Refusing cleanly (rather than silently ignoring a declared `path`) keeps this fail-closed per CLAUDE.md rather than shipping a guessed-at behaviour.

untouched.divergence: A CONTROL_FAILED repair or TRANSIENT-error retry fallthrough on a PROCESS-mechanism STEP re-enters `_advance_process_call` and re-delegates into the same child scope — but since the child's own attempts are already durable and its run already ended, this idempotently re-observes the same already-ended result rather than genuinely re-running the child's internal logic. A repair attempt on a process call therefore cannot change what the child itself did, only whether the OUTER step's own controls/routing re-evaluate the same translated output.

Building a real "re-run the child" semantics would mean deciding whether that means a brand-new run of the same child process or something else entirely — a real design question the spec's own §9 text does not answer, so nothing was guessed at here.

lessons.maxim: Before adding a second mechanism to resume a recursive, stateless-replay engine's paused work, check whether the existing "every call restarts from the top and replays forward" contract already produces that resumption for free — needing a second mechanism is itself a sign the first one was under-trusted, not that the feature needs one.
lessons.incident: Early design reasoning for this run nearly produced a separate function to "cascade a finished child's completion back up to the parent", distinct from the delegation call that enters the child in the first place. Re-reading `report()`/`decide()`/`skip()`'s own existing behaviour (§12.1: they already restart driving from scratch on every call) showed that restarting from the scope's own top segment and letting replay re-descend into the still-open nested level IS the resumption — delegating fresh and resuming an in-flight call are the same code path, once the PROCESS-mechanism dispatch branch is written to only fire on a record-less or repair-eligible visit.
lessons.destination: src/sulis_workflows/engine/run.py — _drive_scope's own docstring now states this reasoning directly, as the artefact this lesson changed.
lessons.proposed_check: Any future WP-03 work adding PARALLEL/JOIN/FOR_EACH resumption should re-derive whether the same replay-from-top contract already covers it before writing a second resumption path.

ready_now: The engine can run a real, tested Process that calls another process — named or inline — including one whose nested step needs a person or an agent, end to end through next()/report()/decide(). This closes the specific gap asked for.
